formalDefinition: SAT = {Φ | Φ is a satisfiable Boolean formula in CNF}
problemDefinition: SAT is the Boolean satisfiability problem for formulas in conjunctive normal form (CNF): a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. It asks whether there is an assignment of True/False values to the variables of Φ that makes the whole formula True. This is Karp's formulation; satisfiability of an arbitrary Boolean formula reduces to it (Tseitin).
inputDescription: Φ, a Boolean formula in CNF
outputDescription: True or False, whether Φ is satisfiable
source: Karp, Richard M. Reducibility among combinatorial problems. Complexity of computer computations. Springer, Boston, MA, 1972. 85-103.
instanceFormat: Boolean formula in CNF. Clauses joined by '&', literals within a clause joined by '|', negation prefix '!' written directly before the name. Variable names start with a letter or '_' and contain only letters, digits and '_'. When there are several clauses, each clause with more than one literal must be in parentheses. Each clause has 1+ literals of any size. Example: (x1 | !x2 | x3) & (!x1 | x2)
certificateFormat: Comma-separated variable:value pairs, optionally wrapped in parentheses. Booleans must be capitalized True/False (T/F also accepted); ':' or '=' may be used as the separator. List every variable you are assigning. Example: (x1:True,x2:False,x3:True)
